data.DisplayText: Get help if you're finding college or sixth form hard
data.Author: [js: parameters('AdminUsername')]

Value.Text: Get help if you’re finding college or sixth form hard

HtmlBodyPart.Html: Things in college or sixth form do not always go to plan. See who can help you decide what to do next, change subjects or pass your GCSE maths or English resit.

How this tool can help you

55% of young people have said something would stop them asking for help.

Taking that step can be hard, especially if you're not sure who the right person to speak to is.

We can help you understand who to speak to.

Who would find this useful

This tool is for young people who are having a hard time in college or sixth form.

You might find this useful if you’re:

  • not sure what to do when you leave college or sixth form
  • on a course you’re not enjoying or did not choose
  • stuck resitting GCSE maths or English over and over again

If any of this feels familiar, you're not on your own. Lots of young people are in a similar situation.

What to expect

You'll answer a few questions. Some questions are optional, such as your name. You can choose what you feel comfortable sharing.

It will take less than 5 minutes to complete.

At the end, you’ll get:

  • advice about what you can do
  • advice on who to speak to
  • suggestions of what to say or how to ask for help

data.DisplayText: I'm not sure what to do when I leave college
data.Author: [js: parameters('AdminUsername')]

Value.Text: I'm not sure what to do when I leave college

HtmlBodyPart.Html: It's normal to feel confused if you're not sure what to do when you leave college. It's okay for your plans to change or for you to change your mind.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Who to speak to and when

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
You'll find it useful to talk to someone you trust. This might be a close friend or someone in your family.

Or you might want to talk to someone at college who knows your situation and the options available.

Careers adviser

Your college will have a careers adviser you can speak to. They can help you look at your options for next year and what might suit you.

Student support services

Most colleges have a student support team who can listen to how you're feeling. This might include pastoral officers and wellbeing or mental health support staff. They might be called something different at your college. If you're not sure you can ask a teacher.

Any teacher or member of staff

It's okay to speak to any teacher or member of staff you feel comfortable with. For example, you might prefer to speak to your personal tutor if you know them well.

Learning support or SEND department

You might feel that you're finding it difficult to think about your next step because of a learning difficulty, neurodivergence or disability. You can speak to a staff member who works in the learning support or special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) department. If you're not sure who this might be, you can ask your tutor for advice.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Think about why you're not sure what to do next

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
It's hard to decide what to do after college. It can feel like a massive decision. You might find it useful to think of it as a choice for now. It's not a permanent decision and you can change your mind if it does not feel right.

It can help to think about what's going on in your life that's making it harder to decide.

For example:

  • you had a plan, but you've changed your mind
  • you feel pressured to choose a specific course or go to uni
  • you're not sure you're going to get the grades you need
  • you're resitting GCSE maths or English and not sure how it might affect your next step

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Understand what your options

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
It can be quite daunting to think about what to do next where there are so many choices.

The National Careers Service has advice about your options when you leave college at 18. Try to look at one option at a time and write down anything you're not sure of. You can then take your questions to a teacher or careers adviser at college.

Or if you can, speak to a careers adviser at college when looking at the options. They can listen to how you feel, understand your situation and go through the options that best suit you.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: What you can ask

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
It can be hard to know how to take the first step of asking for help.

Here are a few prompts of what to say to a tutor or teacher if you're struggling to decide what to do after college:

“Can I talk to you about my plan for after college?”

“I don't want to go to uni. What other options are there I can do?”

“What are my options if I've not passed GCSE maths?”

“Are there any organisations that can help me after I leave college?”

data.DisplayText: I want to switch to a different course at college
data.Author: [js: parameters('AdminUsername')]

Value.Text: I want to switch to a different course at college

HtmlBodyPart.Html: It takes a lot to realise you need to change direction. Whether you've started a course you did not want to do, or have changed your mind, it's okay to talk about it.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Who to speak to and when

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Course teacher

You should speak to your course teacher as soon as possible. They will tell you how to switch course and how the process works in your college.

Any teacher or member of staff

If you prefer, it's okay to speak to any teacher or member of staff you feel comfortable with. For example, you might prefer to speak to your personal tutor first. They'll listen and can help you find out who the right person to speak to is.

Student support services

Your college will likely have a pastoral officer as part of their student support services if you'd rather talk to them about how you're feeling. They might be called something different at your college. If you're not sure, you can ask a teacher.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Think about why you want to change course

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
If you know you want to switch, your teacher might need you to put your request in writing.

You may be able to switch course up to October half term, depending on the subject and qualification. After this, it might be difficult to catch up on missed work.

Your teacher will check if: 

  • you can switch or if it’s too late in the year 
  • you meet the entry requirements of the course 
  • the course you want to do has space or if you can be added to a waiting list  
  • switching would cause any clashes with your other lessons 
  • there's space on a course at a different college 

If you’re doing A levels, you might be able to switch to another subject. Or, you might be able to drop a subject if that’s right for you. Your teacher will help see if this will impact your next step after college.

If you do switch courses, you might have a meeting about it. A parent, carer or family member can come with you if you’d find that helpful – you get to decide.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: What to do if it’s too late in the year to switch

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
It’s okay to be disappointed if it’s too late in the year to switch. Your teacher will explain your options so you can create a plan.

You can ask if you can enrol onto a new course next September. If you'll be 19 or over when starting a new course, it's a good idea to check your funding options early. There may be different types of support available. 

In the meantime, you might want to speak to your college careers adviser. They can help you:

  • explore your options and think about what course or career might be a better fit for you 
  • find out about work experience or volunteering in the subject you’re interested in
  • see how what you're learning on your course might still be useful

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: What you can ask

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Here are a few prompts of what to say to a teacher about wanting to change course:

“Can you explain to me how switching courses works?”

“I want to change course. Are you the best person to speak to about that, or is there someone else I should speak to in college?”

“Can you help me work out what to do if I want to enrol on a new course next September?”

“How do I make an appointment with a careers adviser?”

data.DisplayText: I’m stuck on a course I do not like
data.Author: [js: parameters('AdminUsername')]

Value.Text: I'm stuck on a course I do not like

HtmlBodyPart.Html: If your course is not what you hoped for, you're not alone. Even if you cannot change now, it can still help you build skills for your next step.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: If your course is not what you expected

HtmlBodyPart.Html: It's common to start a course and find it's not quite what you expected. It can feel like dropping out is easier than continuing. It's okay if your path is not straightforward.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Who to speak to and when

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Speak to someone when you feel ready to talk about it. You do not need to speak to everyone – start by choosing one person you feel most comfortable with.

Subject teacher

Speak to your subject teacher if you're struggling with the work, not sure why the course matters or want to know what topics are coming next. They can explain how the course links to jobs, apprenticeships, training or further study. They can also help you get extra support.

A teacher or member of staff

If you prefer, it's okay to speak to any teacher or member of staff you feel comfortable with. For example, you might prefer to speak to your personal tutor first. They'll listen and can help you find out who the right person to speak to is.

Student support services

Your college or sixth form will likely have a pastoral officer as part of their student support services who you can talk to about how you're feeling. They can help if your course is affecting your mood, confidence, attendance or motivation.

Careers adviser

A careers adviser can help you look at your options for next year and help you to understand what your current course can lead to. They can also help you plan steps towards the career, course, apprenticeship or training you want.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Things you can gain from any course

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Staying on your course can still be worthwhile, even if it does not feel useful right now.

You may gain:

  • a qualification that might help you apply for another course, apprenticeship, training or work
  • experience dealing with a difficult situation and asking for support when you need it
  • confidence from seeing the progress you make, even if the course is not your long-term plan
  • practical or technical skills you can use after college or sixth form
  • skills like communication, organisation, problem-solving, teamwork and time management

It may help to think of this course as one part of your plan, not your whole future.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: How to keep going when motivation is low

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Motivation can be harder when you are studying something you do not enjoy. Try to focus on small things you can do.

You could try:

  • setting one small goal, like attending the next lesson
  • using a routine that works for you, for example setting a regular time to do coursework
  • making time for things you enjoy
  • linking assignments or projects to something you're interested in if possible
  • speaking to someone if it's affecting your mood, attendance or ability to complete work

If you have time and it's manageable, you could look for volunteering, an online course, or a club linked to what you want to do next.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: What you can ask

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
It's okay to feel nervous to say how you feel. You do not have to explain everything at once. Start by saying that you're not enjoying the course and would like help thinking about what to do next.

If you are not sure how to start the conversation, you could say:

“I'm not enjoying this course. Can we talk about what I can do?”

"I'm not sure this course is right for me. Can you help me understand my options?"

“Is there any extra support I can get while I finish this course?”

“Who else should I speak to about making a plan?”

You may not be able to change course immediately, but you can still make choices and have some control over what happens next.

data.DisplayText: I’m struggling to pass my college course
data.Author: [js: parameters('AdminUsername')]

Value.Text: I’m struggling to pass my college course

HtmlBodyPart.Html: Find out who to speak to and what your options are if you’re worried about passing.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Who to speak to and when

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Course tutor

You should speak to your tutor as soon as possible. They'll be able to offer advice on specific things you could do to help.

Any teacher or member of staff

If you prefer, it's okay to speak to any teacher or member of staff you feel comfortable with. For example, you might prefer to speak to your personal tutor first. They can listen to you and help you to create a plan.

Student support services

Your college will likely have a pastoral officer as part of their student support services if you'd rather talk to them about how you're feeling. They might be called something different at your college. If you're not sure, you can ask a teacher.

Learning support or SEND department

You might feel that you're finding things difficult because of a learning difficulty, neurodivergence or disability. You can speak to a staff member who works in the learning support or special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) department. If you're not sure who this might be, you can ask your tutor for advice.

Careers adviser

A careers adviser can help you understand how different options might affect your future plans. They can also help you think through alternative routes if you're worried about passing your course.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Think about why you're struggling

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
There are many reasons why you might be struggling with one or more of your courses in college.

It could be that you found the subject easier during GCSEs, but it seems to be different or more difficult at college.

This is completely normal and could be due to:

  • the course covering different topics than it did at GCSE
  • the subject is different or harder than you expected
  • new tutors in college, or different teaching styles
  • struggling with essays or exams – you may find coursework more suited to the way you learn, for example
  • something in your personal life that is affecting your studies

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: What you can do next

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Depending on what stage you're at in college, not passing your course can mean different things. It's normal to feel stressed, but there are things you can do that can help.

You may be able to:

  • change your subject or course if it's still early in the academic year
  • drop a course or subject if you're doing more than one so you can reduce your timetable and focus on the courses you feel more confident in
  • swap to another class if there's more than one class of this subject
  • resit anything you did not pass
  • get feedback on assessments you did not pass, so you can focus on what to improve

Your teacher can help you decide what option might suit you best. Think about what's important to you now and for your next step. For example, if you need certain grades or qualifications for further study or job applications. This will help you narrow down what to do.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: What you can ask

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Whoever you choose to talk to, it's a good step towards changing things for the better.

It can be hard knowing how to get the most out of conversations or even how to start them.

Here are a few prompts of what to say to a tutor or teacher if you're struggling to pass your course at college:

“I am struggling to pass this course. Are you the best person to speak to about that, or is there someone else I should speak to in college?”

“Can you help me work out what to do or what will happen if I want to drop this course?”

“What are my options if I don't pass my resits?”

“Is it possible for me to drop or change one of my courses or subjects?”

data.DisplayText: I need to pass my GCSE maths resit
data.Author: [js: parameters('AdminUsername')]

Value.Text: I need to pass my GCSE maths resit

HtmlBodyPart.Html: It can be tough having to keep resitting your maths GCSE. You're not the only one. Over 200,000 young people in England sat their maths GCSE again in 2025.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Understand what you're struggling with

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Have a think about what part of the resit is stressing you out. You might find it easier to ask for help about something specific.

Think about:

  • whether you're missing out on passing by only a few marks
  • if your nerves are taking over on exam day
  • if you're struggling to answer questions on specific topics

If you want to see your completed exam paper, contact your school or college as soon as possible after receiving your results. There may be deadlines and fees to do this.

Whether or not you review your paper, your maths teacher can help you understand which topics to focus on before you resit.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Who to speak to and when

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Your GCSE maths teacher

You should let your maths teacher know as soon as possible that you want help. They can create a plan with you about what to focus on for your resit.

Any teacher or member of staff

If you prefer, it's okay to speak to any teacher or member of staff you feel comfortable with. They can listen and help you to create a plan.

Student support services

Your college or sixth form will likely have a pastoral or support team you can speak to for help with your resit. They can also help if your resit is affecting your confidence, motivation or wellbeing.

Maths tutor

You could get tutoring from someone familiar with your exam paper. Your teacher might know older students who have recently passed the exam who can help. Or, if you're able to pay, they might be able to recommend a local or online tutor.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Alternative to GCSE maths

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
If you're struggling to pass after several resits, you might be able to do a Functional Skills level 2 qualification instead. This is equivalent to a GCSE grade 4 pass and is often accepted as an alternative to a GCSE.

Your maths teacher or student support services can help see if you're eligible to do a functional skills course. You can find out more functional skills qualifications from Prospects.

You might plan to start another course, apprenticeship or training after college or sixth form. If so, a careers adviser can help you find out if a functional skills qualification would be accepted instead of a GCSE.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: Understand your options after college or sixth form

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Your maths teacher or student support services can help you understand what your options are if you do or do not pass maths.

It's normal to be worried and want a plan. There are options if you need to do your maths resit after college. GCSE maths courses are often available in libraries, adult education centres or other local venues.

You might want to speak to a careers adviser so you can chat about what you want to do. They can help you create a plan to get there.

GdsAccordionSectionPart.Title: What you can ask

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
Here are a few prompts of what to say to get help with your maths resit:

“Are there any resources I can use that are different from what I've already tried?”

“Can I get any further help or tutoring to help me pass?”

“Can you show me why my answer to this question did not work?”

data.DisplayText: Accessibility statement
data.Author: [js: parameters('AdminUsername')]

HtmlBodyPart.Html:
This accessibility statement applies to the Get help if you’re finding college or sixth form hard prototype.

This prototype is run by the Department for Education. We want as many people as possible to be able to use this prototype. For example, that means you should be able to:

  • change colours, contrast levels and fonts using browser or device settings
  • zoom in up to 400% without the text spilling off the screen
  • navigate most of the prototype using a keyboard or speech recognition software
  • listen to most of the prototype using a screen reader (including the most recent versions of JAWS, NVDA and VoiceOver)

We’ve also made the prototype text as simple as possible to understand.

AbilityNet has advice on making your device easier to use if you have a disability.

How accessible this prototype is

We know some parts of this website are not fully accessible:

  • No nav landmark. The page does not explicitly identify the primary navigation content using ARIA role="nav" or the HTML element.
  • Links do not have accessible names.
  • The <textarea> form control does not have an associated <label> element, and Table headers not correctly marking up.
  • The ‘Department for Education’ logo does not have visible keyboard focus.
  • The links within the footer of the service do not respond to text resizing.

Feedback and contact information

If you find any problems not listed on this page or think we’re not meeting accessibility requirements, contact: NationalCareersService.PMO@education.gov.uk

Enforcement procedure

The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) is responsible for enforcing the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018 (the ‘accessibility regulations’). If you’re not happy with how we respond to your complaint, contact the Equality Advisory and Support Service (EASS) .

Technical information about this prototype’s accessibility

The Department for Education is committed to making its prototypes accessible, in accordance with the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018.

Compliance status

The website has been tested against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 AA standard.

This website is partially compliant with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines version 2.2 AA standard, due to the non-compliances listed below.

Non-accessible content

The content listed below is non-accessible for the following reasons.

Non-compliance with the accessibility regulations

  • No nav landmark. The page does not explicitly identify the primary navigation content using ARIA role="nav" or the HTML element. WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion: 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks. We plan to make sure there is a nav landmark.
  • Links do not have accessible names. WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.4: Link Purpose (In Context). We plan to make sure all links have accessible names.
  • The <textarea> form control does not have an associated <label> element, and table headers not correctly marking up. WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1: Info and Relationships. We plan to make sure the form control does not have the associated label element, and we plan to mark up table headings.
  • The ‘Department for Education’ logo does not have visible keyboard focus. WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7 - Focus Visible – Level AA.
  • The links within the footer of the service do not respond to text resizing. WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.4 - Resize text – Level AA.

We plan to fix these accessibility issues by September 2026 to make sure we're compliant.

Preparation of this accessibility statement

This statement was prepared on 7 August 2026.

This prototype was last tested on 3 August 2026 against the WCAG 2.2 AA standard. The test was carried out by an internal team in the Department for Education.
We're testing this website. Help improve it by completing a short feedback form (opens in a new tab) .

Essential cookies

Analytics cookies (optional)
